The party purchasing land over which surface water naturally flows assumes the burden of receiving such surface water and connot obstruct, impede, or stop such natural drainage to the injury of the owner of the dominant land.
2. Parties Subject to Drainage Rules
Drainage rules, in general, recognize the Division as a landowner and, consequently, they apply equally to the Division and individual landowner. One exception is that the Division may use eminent domain laws of the State to acquire property or rights to perform necessary functions of drainage.
The Division does not have the responsibility of providing drainage to protect adjacent landowners from the natural overflow of water unless the need for such drainage results from their acts. Conversely the Division cannot cause the land of the adjacent owners to be overflowed to a greater extent than it has been in the natural state.
WATERCOURSES CARRYING SURFACE WATERS
1. Watercourse
The line of flow where surface water moves uniformly or habitually over a given course with reasonable width limits is considered a watercourse. A natural watercourse is one whose origin is the result of the forces of nature. An artificial watercourse owes its origin to acts of man and includes drainage ditches, canals, etc. An artificial watercourse may be considered a natural watercourse when it has served in lieu of a natural channel for a prescribed period, and it has all the essential elements of a watercourse. Therefore, when drainage ditches have been constructed by common consent and used for the prescribed period, they become watercourses as fully as though they were not of artificial origin.
